paragraphs: But according to the drift of the reasoning by which women are kept from the tree of knowledge, the important years of youth, the usefulness of age and the rational hopes of a life to come are all to be sacrificed to make woman an object of desire for a short time. Besides, how could Rousseau expect women to be virtuous and constant when reason is neither allowed to be the foundation of their virtue nor truth the object of their inquiries?

But all Rousseau’s errors in reasoning arose from sensibility — and sensibility to their charms women are very ready to forgive! When he should have reasoned, he became impassioned, and reflection inflamed his imagination instead of enlightening his understanding. Even his virtues led him further astray; for, born with a warm constitution and a lively imagination, he was carried by nature toward the other sex with such eager fondness that he soon became lascivious. Had he given way to these desires, the fire would have burned itself out naturally; but virtue, and a romantic kind of delicacy, made him practise self-denial. Yet when fear, delicacy or virtue held him back, he debauched his imagination; and, dwelling on the sensations to which fancy gave force, he traced them in the most glowing colours and sank them deep into his soul.

He then sought solitude — not to sleep with the man of nature, or calmly to investigate the causes of things in the shade where Sir Isaac Newton gave himself up to contemplation, but merely to indulge his feelings. And he has painted what he felt so forcibly with such warmth that, by engaging the hearts and inflaming the imaginations of his readers, he leads them, in proportion to the strength of their fancy, to imagine that their understanding is convinced, when they are only sympathizing with a poetic writer who skilfully displays the objects of the senses, most voluptuously shaded or gracefully veiled. And so, as he makes us feel while we dream that we are reasoning, mistaken conclusions are left in the mind.

Why was Rousseau’s life divided between ecstasy and misery? Can any other answer be given than that the effervescence of his imagination produced both? Had his fancy been allowed to cool, it is possible that he might have acquired more strength of mind. Still, if the purpose of life is to educate the intellectual part of man, everything concerning him was right; yet, had death not led to a nobler scene of action, he would probably have enjoyed a more even happiness on earth, and felt the calm sensations of the man of nature, instead of being prepared for another stage of existence by nourishing the passions that agitate civilized man.
But peace to his spirit! I do not make war on his ashes, but on his opinions. I make war only on the sensibility that led him to degrade woman by making her the slave of love.
....“Curs’d vassalage, First idoliz’d till love’s hot fire be o’er, Then slaves to those who courted us before.” Dryden.
The harmful tendency of those books in which the writers insidiously degrade the sex while they lie prostrate before women’s personal charms cannot be exposed too often or too severely.

Let us, my dear contemporaries, rise above such narrow prejudices! If wisdom is desirable for its own sake, if virtue, to deserve the name, must be founded on knowledge, let us try to strengthen our minds by reflection until our heads become a counterweight to our hearts. Let us not confine all our thoughts to the petty events of the day, nor our knowledge to an acquaintance with the hearts of our lovers or husbands; but let the practice of every duty be subordinate to the great one of improving our minds and preparing our affections for a more exalted state!
Beware, then, my friends, of letting the heart be moved by every trivial incident: the reed is shaken by a breeze and dies every year, but the oak stands firm and braves the storm for ages.

If we were indeed created only to flutter out our hour and die — why, then, let us indulge sensibility and laugh at the severity of reason. Yet, alas! even then we should lack strength of body and mind, and life would be lost in feverish pleasures or wearisome languor.

But the system of education that I earnestly wish to see discredited seems to presuppose what ought never to be taken for granted: that virtue shields us from the accidents of life, and that fortune, slipping off her blindfold, will smile on a well-educated woman and bring her an Emilius or a Telemachus by the hand. On the contrary, the reward that virtue promises her devotees is clearly confined to their own hearts; and they must often struggle with the most vexing worldly cares and put up with the vices and moods of relations for whom they can never feel friendship.

There have been many women in the world who, instead of being supported by the reason and virtue of their fathers and brothers, have strengthened their own minds by struggling with their vices and follies, and yet have never met with a hero in the shape of a husband who, paying the debt that mankind owed them, might happen to bring their reason back to its natural dependent state and restore to man the usurped prerogative of rising above opinion.
